Dear Colleagues,

sorry for cross-posting and for the follow up, but for the method mentioned
below and when DISTANCE Sampling would be applied, I wonder how these could
deal with the responsive movement bias, e.g. when spot-lighting is done and
when cars driving on gravel roads are used.

We know the expected frequency distribution before disturbance and
afterwards (from DISTANCE); could that be used to correct abundances and
still obtain
decent abundance estimates with confidence? The responsive movement I am
dealing with is basically just a consistent distance offset by app. 50m
(short distance escape/avoidance).

Thanks very much for any advice; it's a key question for us.

Kind regards

F.

Jeff- Spotlighting off-road has been done by black-footed ferret biologists
at night for years. It could likely be applied to any nocturnal furbearer
that could be approached within a few hundred meters at night. We did this
with deep cycling marine 12 v. batteries on backpack frames, using hand-held
spotlights (candlepower will depend on how far you need to project a light
source with respect to terrain, vegetation, etc.). We picked up coyotes,
badgers and porcupines on a regular basis. The deep cycling rechargable
marine batteries were good for an entire night (8+ hours) of continuous
operation. Hope this helps.
